narrative:
The 2017 New York Mets were supposed to be contenders. Coming off back-to-back postseason appearances, the roster was loaded with pitching talent and offensive firepower, and expectations ran high in Flushing. Instead, what unfolded was a season of cascading misfortune — injuries to key pitchers, bullpen implosions, and an August collapse that effectively buried any lingering hope. The Mets finished 70-92, one of the franchise's ugliest records in recent memory.

April set the tone in the worst possible way. The bullpen hemorrhaged leads with alarming regularity, as relievers Fernando Salas, Addison Reed, and Josh Edgin surrendered critical home runs and doubles that turned wins into losses. Amid the carnage, Jay Bruce provided the season's earliest genuine bright spots, blasting go-ahead home runs on April 10 and April 19 that briefly sparked optimism. But the month closed at 10-14, a damning verdict on a roster that couldn't keep leads intact.

May and June offered a modest steadying, with the team playing close to .500 and showing flashes of the offense that was supposed to carry them. Neil Walker's clutch single on May 8 and Asdrubal Cabrera's booming home run on July 1 were reminders of what this lineup could do when healthy. July brought a few signature moments — Wilmer Flores going deep, Curtis Granderson providing pop — but the team still hovered around mediocrity, unable to string together consistent winning.

August was the season's death knell. The Mets went a catastrophic 10-20, their rotation decimated by injuries and their bullpen incapable of protecting any lead. By September, the games were largely meaningless, yet the bullpen continued to find new ways to fail, surrendering late leads to the Marlins and others down the stretch. Asdrubal Cabrera's three-run homer on the season's final day on September 30 was a bittersweet punctuation mark — a flash of what might have been in a season that never came close to fulfilling its promise.

chapters.title: Broken from the Start
chapters.description: A miserable April sees the bullpen surrender leads night after night, with only Jay Bruce's big swings offering any relief.

chapters.title: Treading Water
chapters.description: May and early June bring sporadic clutch moments and a near-.500 pace, but the team can never fully right the ship.

chapters.title: Summer Sparks
chapters.description: July produces some of the season's most memorable individual moments, with Cabrera, Granderson, Flores, and Reyes delivering timely heroics.

chapters.title: The August Collapse
chapters.description: A 10-20 August crushes any remaining playoff hopes as injuries and bullpen failures combine for the season's most devastating stretch.

chapters.title: Playing Out the String
chapters.description: September's meaningless games still find the bullpen imploding, though Cabrera's final-day home run offers a fleeting glimpse of what could have been.
